candidate.answerReason: Each adjacent overlap has area \(\pi/3-\sqrt{3}/4\). Subtracting the three small semicircle areas from the large semicircle and restoring both overlaps gives \(7\pi/6-\sqrt{3}/2\), agreeing with E.

methods.label: Correct for overlapping semicircles
methods.explanation:
[Figure 1](figures/2003_AMC_10B_Q19_question_fig1.svg)

Subtracting the three small semicircle areas would remove their overlapping parts twice, so we first find the area of one overlap.

Let \(O_1,O_2,O_3\) be the small semicircle centers in order from \(A\) to \(B\). Since \(AB=4\), the four equal gaps each have length \(1\), and \(O_2\) is also the large semicircle's center. Each small center is at most \(1\) from \(O_2\), so every point in a small semicircle is at most \(1+1=2\) from \(O_2\). All semicircles lie on the same side of \(AB\), so the small ones lie entirely inside the large one.

For an adjacent pair, call the centers \(X,Y\), and let \(P\) be their arc intersection above \(AB\). The lengths \(XY,XP,YP\) are all \(1\), so \(\triangle XYP\) is equilateral and its angles are \(60^\circ\). Its altitude bisects its base, giving height
\[
\sqrt{1-\left(\frac12\right)^2}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.
\]
Its area is therefore \(\sqrt3/4\).

The two \(60^\circ\) sectors with centers \(X\) and \(Y\) cover the overlap, sharing exactly \(\triangle XYP\). Thus the overlap area is
\[
L=2\left(\frac{60}{360}\pi\right)-\frac{\sqrt3}{4}
=\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\sqrt3}{4}.
\]
There are two congruent adjacent overlaps. The outer two semicircles touch only at \(O_2\), so they have no common area, and there is no triple overlap of positive area.

We can now subtract all three small areas and restore the two parts removed twice:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S&=\frac12\pi(2)^2-3\left(\frac12\pi(1)^2\right)+2L\\
&=2\pi-\frac{3\pi}{2}+\frac{2\pi}{3}-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\
&=\boxed{\frac{7\pi}{6}-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The answer is choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
